docs.text: Function Purpose exactQuantity Requires exactly one asset under a policy with the expected quantity tokenFromPolicy Extracts the sole asset name under a specific policy carriesStateToken Authenticates a state UTxO by (statePolicyId, cageToken) validateOwnership Owner signature, plus a stake_script withdrawal when one is set in_phase1 Checks the oracle processing window in_phase2 Checks the requester retract window is_rejectable Checks Phase 3 or dishonest future submitted_at processableRequest Defines which request UTxOs are protected from Sweep

docs.title: Permissionless multi-oracle registries
docs.text:
Design stage

This section describes a design that is decided, modelled in Lean and independently audited, but not yet implemented in the validators. The shipped cage is described under Architecture. Implementation is tracked by the milestone Permissionless multi-oracle registries.

docs.title: Who this is for
docs.text:
As anyone who wants a shared, verifiable key-value registry on Cardano, I want to create one by naming the oracles that judge it and the protocol they judge, so that I need no script, no owner and no folding infrastructure of my own, and anyone can fold what my oracles have approved.

The shipped cage has a single privileged party: its owner is the only one who can fold requests into the tree, and a per-cage request script holds every request. This design removes both. A registry becomes a piece of data that names its judges; one request script per release serves every registry; and folding becomes a permissionless service anyone can offer.

The people involved and what each one gets:

Who Wants Sees when it works Sees when it is refused Registry creator A registry whose rules are fixed forever A registry state with an empty tree, its oracles, its protocol and optionally a rule Creation fails if the registry has neither an oracle nor a rule, or repeats an oracle Requester One write applied under conditions they choose Their write folded into the tree, their fees paid to the oracles, the rest bid to the folder A refusal, or a fold whose conditions do not hold; after the deadline they settle and recover the rest Oracle To be paid for judging, whatever it decides Its fee credited to its balance at the fold, or at the complete account after the deadline, and collected by claim when it chooses Nothing to refuse: an oracle that does not serve a registry simply never answers Folder To earn the remainder of requests it folds Approved requests applied, the remainder of each request paid to it A fold with a missing approval, a false condition or a late time is rejected Reader The registry's current contents The tree rebuilt by replaying folds, with every write in a request datum Nothing hidden: every write and every judgment is on chain

docs.title: The system at a glance
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  creator([Registry creator]) -- "mints, naming oracles and protocol" --> state[(Registry state:<br/>root, oracles, protocol)]
  requester([Requester]) -- "creates request, mints one tag<br/>per oracle, escrows fees" --> request[(Request output<br/>at the release request address)]
  oracle([Each oracle]) -- "reads request, judges off chain,<br/>mints approval or refusal" --> judgment[(Judgment token<br/>in the oracle's wallet)]
  folder([Folder]) -- "spends requests, reads judgments,<br/>proves conditions" --> state
  request -- "consumed by fold,<br/>settlement or withdrawal" --> folder
  judgment -. "referenced, never spent" .-> folder
  reader([Reader]) -- "replays folds" --> state

The registry state is the one output on chain that holds a registry's root hash, its rules and its fee balances; the shipped design calls it the cage. Every arrow into the registry state goes through the fold. Judgments are minted by reference to the request, so oracles never compete for the same output. The request output is spent exactly once, by one of three exits, each in its own time window.

docs.title: Reading route
docs.text:
1. Open MPFS design document: every decision in one place, with its status.
  2. Request lifecycle: the states of a request, its three time windows and a sequence diagram for every exit.
  3. Decisions: every design choice with the alternatives it rejected and why.
  4. Economics: who pays whom, the markets this opens, and the shipped cage as a special case.
  5. Oracle identities: oracles as keys or groups with shares, and how fees reach each key.
  6. Oracle slots and check protocols, a draft: which oracle judges which keys under which published check, worked through on the moog registry.
  7. Formal model and audits: what is proved in Lean, what the independent audits found, and what is not yet covered.

The authoritative decision record is specs/request-approval-fold/decisions.md; these pages explain it.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
As a reviewer of this design, I want every choice next to the alternatives it rejected, so that I can judge the reasoning and not only the result.

The decisions were taken in October 2026, starting from the Singular investigation in which the request lifecycle belongs to the application (lambdasistemi/singular#731, #741). The design went through a single-oracle version, a multi-oracle version, two independent audits and one repair; the tables below record what each step taught. The authoritative record is specs/request-approval-fold/decisions.md.

docs.title: Who checks what
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  requester([Requester]) -- "states the write and<br/>the conditions on the tree" --> request[(Request)]
  oracles([Oracles]) -- "judge off chain that the requester<br/>may ask for it (tree-independent)" --> request
  folder([Folder]) -- "proves the write applies<br/>to the tree now" --> tree[(Tree)]
  request --> folder
Decision Chosen Rejected Why What an oracle judges Authorization of the request, independent of the tree (for Moog: GitHub keys, repository roles, signatures) Judging the change against the current root Any fold changes the root while an oracle is deciding; a tree-bound approval would go stale before it could be used Where tree validity is checked At the fold, by conditions on any key, against the tree reached when the request is applied Binding the request to the root it was created against A request bound to one root dies at the next fold, so an oracle's work would be wasted whenever anyone else folds first What a request may write One set key value or unset key, plus conditions key absent or key equals value Only the shipped compare-and-swap operations Compare-and-swap is a write with a condition on its own key; conditions on other keys let applications state rules a generic registry cannot foresee Who folds Anyone Only the oracle or owner Folding needs no knowledge of the application, so it can be a generic service across every registry Externalized per-key state, as in Singular Out of scope; everything stays in the tree Generalizing one design to cover both Per-key tokens minted and burned at the fold are a different system; combining both would complicate each

docs.title: Registries
docs.text: Decision Chosen Rejected Why Who may create a registry Anyone, by minting a registry state that names its oracles and protocol Creating a cage that applies a per-cage script No script per registry means nothing to publish or audit per registry How many oracles Any number, every one of which must approve; at least one oracle or a rule One oracle per registry; at least one oracle in every registry Different oracles check different things, so applications are composed from oracles. A registry with a rule needs no oracle: a rule admitting one owner gives a personal registry anyone can fold Changing the oracle set Never: the oracles and the protocol are the registry's identity An owner who can change it; changes approved by the current oracles Every entry means "judged by these oracles under this protocol"; changing them leaves part of the tree judged one way and part another, and no migration repairs that Owner, end, transfer None An owner who can end or freeze the registry The oracles are the only judges and they only judge requests; a central power above distributed judgment makes no sense. A registry whose oracles stop answering simply stops moving Oracle consent to being listed Not needed Requiring oracles to sign the registry Listing is an offer of business; an oracle that does not serve a registry never answers it What an oracle is An identity of the oracle standard: a key, or a group with a threshold and a share per member; the registry names it by the hash of its description A single key per oracle; a script credential per oracle A single key is lost with its key; a script oracle could only be seen acting through a zero withdrawal or by spending its own output. See Oracle identities What the oracles understand The registry names a protocol by hash: a CDDL document for keys, values and evidence No declared protocol An oracle cannot judge a request whose meaning it does not know; the protocol affects progress, never safety

docs.title: Requests
docs.text: Decision Chosen Rejected Why Where requests live One request script per release, serving every registry, as spending validator and minting policy A request script applied per cage (shipped); requests held in the requester's own wallet A per-cage script publishes one address per registry; a request in a wallet cannot be forced into the fold, which must spend it Replay protection A seed: an output reference spent by the creating transaction Nothing beyond the request contents Two identical requests would let one approval be reused for the other Where the write lives On chain in the request datum, paid by the requester Off chain behind a hash Readers rebuild the tree by replaying folds at no cost. A protocol may still store a hash as the value and leave its preimage to the key holder Where the oracles' evidence lives An opaque field; the protocol decides whether it holds the evidence or its hash Forcing one or the other On chain lets anyone audit the oracles' reasons; off chain is cheaper. Both have uses Lifetime A deadline and a window, chosen by the requester Withdrawal at any time Oracles that already judged would lose their fee to a requester who leaves; enough such requests starve the oracles

docs.title: Judgments and discovery
docs.text: Decision Chosen Rejected Why How an oracle approves Mints an approval token, with the request output as a reference input, into any output (typically its own wallet) Minting into the request output, which spends it; one voucher output per oracle at the script Spending the request makes several oracles race for one output; vouchers put several extra outputs per request at the script What a judgment's name binds The registry, the request with its seed, the oracle, the verdict, the signing members of a group oracle and an approval's conditions The registry and request only Without oracle and verdict, approvals and refusals from different oracles would collide Approval expiry None: the request's deadline bounds every judgment An expiry chosen by the oracle, with a minimum window protecting the requester Once fees are paid only at the fold, a late or short-lived approval costs the requester nothing; an oracle that finds a deadline too far for its judgment simply does not answer How oracles find work One tag per oracle, minted with the request and named after the oracle; one asset query finds an oracle's work across every registry One tag named after the registry; inspecting the address's staking part A registry tag forces each oracle to index every registry that names it; the staking-part trick was declined as obscure How folders find work The request token: one query per registry lists its live requests; approvals, whose names bind the oracle's conditions, are found by listing the judgment outputs and reading their datums Computing approval names in advance, impossible once they bind conditions; a separate index A registry without oracles has no approvals; the request token covers every registry and every live request An oracle answering both ways Accepted, not prevented A ballot per oracle minted with the request and burned at judgment, so each oracle can answer once Under one exit per window, equivocation changes no payment and no outcome; the two verdicts stay on chain under the oracle's signature, so it is public and provable. Ballots would add one output per oracle to every request

docs.title: Rules, request tokens and oracle conditions
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  requester([Requester]) -- "conditions: its intent" --> request[(Request)]
  rule([Registry rule, at creation]) -- "demands conditions,<br/>mints the request token" --> request
  oracle([Each oracle, at approval]) -- "adds conditions<br/>bound in the approval's name" --> approval[(Approval)]
  request --> fold([Fold])
  approval --> fold
  fold -- "proves every condition<br/>at the request's turn" --> tree[(Tree)]
Decision Chosen Rejected Why Where a registry's on-chain rules live A compiled minting policy named by hash in the registry state, minting the request token at creation A fixed vocabulary of rules built into the release; a rule program interpreted by the fold; a rule run by the fold through a zero withdrawal Registries are immutable, so a fixed vocabulary would lock each to its release; an interpreter costs fold budget; at the fold the rule would traverse every batch, while everything it checks is fixed in the request at creation How a rule constrains the tree It demands conditions in the request; the fold proves them Letting the rule read the tree The tree is a root hash; the fold already proves conditions at the right point of the batch, so the rule validates the program and the fold executes it The condition language absent, present, equals Predicates on values; facts about key prefixes Each construct is a permanent cost in the fold; value predicates wait until a registry needs them, and per-key proofs cannot establish prefix facts What makes a request genuine A request token per request, minted only through the creation checks and burned by every exit The oracle tags A registry without oracles has no tags; the request token also lists a registry's live requests with one query An oracle whose rules the request's conditions do not cover It approves with its own conditions, bound in the approval's name and proved by the fold at the request's turn Refusing, and the requester re-creating the request The oracle judged against the tree it saw; its conditions make the approval usable only while what it assumed still holds

docs.title: Money and exits
docs.text: Decision Chosen Rejected Why What the requester pays for Judgment, not outcome: approval and refusal pay the same fee A fee only for approval; paid refusal as an opt-in Equal fees make the oracle indifferent between verdicts, so it judges honestly; an oracle paid only to refuse could target a requester When oracles are paid From escrow in the request, credited to a balance per key in the registry state at the fold or the complete account, collected by claim At the first approval (spending the request); paid up front at creation; one payout output per oracle per request Paying at approval reintroduces contention; prepayment pays oracles that never answer; every output must hold the ledger's minimum of ada, so a payout per oracle per request costs a minimum each time and cannot pay a smaller fee How an oracle collects its fees A claim: a request created with the key's signature, naming its payout address and datum and carrying a tip; a fold pays the whole balance at the claim's turn A withdrawal spending the registry state directly; a payout address fixed in the registry by its creator A direct withdrawal races the fold for the registry state; a payout chosen by the registry creator is not the oracle's own choice What may spend the registry state Only a fold, whose items are writes, complete accounts and claims A complete account and a claim as separate transactions Anything else that changes the cage races the fold What happens to the remainder at a fold It is the folder's bid Refunded to the requester No refund outputs per request, so folds batch more requests; the bid is what pays folders Leaving a request that cannot fold A complete account, as an item of a fold: a verdict from every oracle, every oracle's fee credited, the rest to the owner Consuming the request by proving one of its conditions false; letting one approving oracle close it; each oracle taking its fee from the request separately A provable failure can be engineered by approving a conflicting request; one closing oracle can be bribed to omit the others; oracles taking their fees one by one contend for the request When a settlement is allowed Only from the deadline to the deadline plus the window At any time; before the deadline with at least one refusal Any overlap with the fold window creates a race between folder and owner; an early exit on one refusal lets the owner hide the other approvals, or pays oracles that never judged A silent oracle After the window the owner takes everything and may pay those who answered Paying every oracle regardless The chain cannot tell a silent oracle from an approval the owner chooses not to show; a silent oracle losing its fee is the incentive to answer

docs.title: Prices, ordering and encodings
docs.text:
Decision Chosen Rejected Why How a requester learns the price Each oracle keeps an on-chain price notice: a token named after it, minted with its signature, whose datum carries its current fee Prices in the registry's protocol document; prices on each oracle's own endpoint The protocol document is fixed by hash, so prices could never change; private endpoints are neither discoverable nor verifiable. The notice is not binding, but ignoring a request that pays the posted price is public Conflicting approved requests The folder's order decides, and bids can buy it; applications wanting fairness have their oracles approve only one of conflicting requests First come, first served enforced on chain The chain cannot prove that an older approved request was skipped; the losing request costs only its fees, because it settles Oracles holding up a request Accepted: holding out is pricing Fixed prices or a fee cap in the registry An immutable registry would freeze prices forever, and an oracle could still go silent; silence earns nothing and refusal pays the same as approval Encodings Everything in CDDL, describing the Plutus Data encoding, with test vectors pinning exact bytes Hand-built CBOR layouts serialise_data is one cheap builtin; hand-built bytes would be assembled in script code on every mint and burn Hashed token names blake2b-256 of serialise_data of a tuple led by the token's role (tag, approval, refusal, price) Names without a role field 32 bytes is the asset-name maximum; the leading role keeps every kind of token apart

These were settled in #116.

docs.title: Not decided
docs.text:
• the migration or coexistence of existing cages (#117);
  • the fold cost per condition proof and per judgment reference, to be measured on a devnet (#115).

docs.title: Economics
docs.text: As someone deciding whether to run an oracle, fold requests or build an application on a registry, I want to know who pays whom and what each role earns, so that I can tell whether the role is worth taking.

docs.title: Money flows
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  requester([Requester]) -- "escrow: fees for every oracle<br/>plus a bid" --> request[(Request)]
  request -- "fold or complete account:<br/>each oracle's fee" --> cage[(Registry state: one balance per key)]
  request -- "fold: the remainder" --> folder([Folder])
  request -- "complete account: the remainder" --> owner([Request owner])
  request -- "after the window: everything" --> owner
  cage -- "claim, folded when the key chooses:<br/>its whole balance" --> payout([Payout chosen by the key])
Exit Oracles Folder Request owner Fold, before the deadline Each its declared fee, credited to its keys' balances Everything else Nothing back; the write is applied Complete account, as a fold item in the window Each its declared fee, credited, whatever its verdict Nothing Everything else Withdrawal, after the window Whatever the owner chooses to pay Nothing Everything Claim, as a fold item The key's whole balance, to the payout it named The claim's tip Not involved

Fees accumulate in the registry state instead of being paid one output at a time. Every output on chain must hold the ledger's minimum of ada, so a fee per oracle per request in its own output would cost a minimum each time, and a fee below the minimum could not be paid at all. A key pays that minimum once per claim, when its balance is worth collecting. A group oracle's fee is split among its members' keys by the shares in its description, so each member is paid its share without trusting the others.

docs.title: Three markets instead of one
docs.text:
The shipped cage has one business: the owner, which is both the only oracle and the only folder, takes a fixed tip per request. It is a monopoly on its cage, and requests can only leave through it or after a retract window. This design splits that into separate markets:

  • Judgment. Oracles sell verdicts at a price the requester posts, one fee per oracle. An oracle takes the request or ignores it. Because approval and refusal pay the same, an oracle earns by judging, never by choosing a verdict.
  • Folding. Folding needs no knowledge of the application, and one request address per release serves every registry, so a single folder can serve all of them. Competition among folders pushes the bid towards the real cost of a fold: the transaction fee, the proofs and the latency.
  • Ordering. The folder chooses the order of a fold. When two approved requests conflict, for example both setting a key under the condition that it is absent, the order decides which one wins, and bids can buy that order. In the shipped cage this power belonged to the owner. This is accepted: the losing request costs only its fees, and an application that wants fair ordering gets it from its oracles, which can approve only one of conflicting requests.

docs.title: Risks each role carries
docs.text: Role Carries Bounded by Requester Fees paid even when refused; the wait until the deadline if refused or unfoldable Its own choice of fees, deadline and window Oracle Judging work on a request that never folds; a stolen key Payment at the complete account for every verdict; silence is the only unpaid case, and it is the oracle's own. A group oracle survives stolen keys below its threshold Good oracle in a registry with a silent oracle Requests that cannot fold, settled only if the owner pays after the window Its decision to stop serving that registry Folder Losing a race for the registry state to another folder A transaction whose inputs were already spent is rejected before any script runs, and costs nothing Registry creator Choosing oracles that later go silent Nothing: trust is placed in the oracles when they are named; a dead registry is replaced by a new one

docs.title: Several oracles holding up a request
docs.text: When every oracle must approve, each can block a request, and fees are fixed in the request: an oracle cannot raise its price on chain, but it can decline until the requester re-creates the request with a higher fee. Complementary monopolies tend to price the whole above what one integrated oracle would. This is accepted: since silence earns nothing and a refusal pays the same as an approval, holding out is only pricing. To make prices discoverable, each oracle keeps an on-chain price notice: a token named after it whose datum carries its current fee, so a wallet adds up a registry's price with one query per oracle before creating a request. The notice is not binding, but an oracle ignoring requests that pay its posted price contradicts its own signed notice in public.

docs.title: The shipped cage as a special case
docs.text:
Shipped cage In this design The owner is the only oracle and the only folder A registry with one oracle that signs its own folds Insert value set key value with the condition key absent Delete value unset key with the condition key equals value Update old new set key new with the condition key equals old The tip per request The oracle's fee The processing window, then the retract window The deadline, then the settlement window, then the owner's withdrawal Owner can transfer or end the cage No counterpart

Simulating the shipped cage costs a tag minted and burned per request (one oracle, one tag), one more script run per fold transaction, and a larger datum. It costs no extra proof: a condition and a write on the same key share one Merkle Patricia Forestry proof. Conditions on other keys are new, and paid for only when used. Because the remainder of a request goes to the folder, a fold writes no refund output per request, so batches can be larger than today.

docs.title: For applications
docs.text:
• Composition. An application is a registry plus a set of oracles, and it can reuse third-party oracles, such as one identity oracle shared by many registries.
  • No folding infrastructure. An application's requests keep moving while its own machines are down; only judgment depends on it.
  • Censorship. Oracles can still refuse to answer, but no folder can censor an approved request: anyone can fold it.
  • Rules on other keys. Conditions let an application express invariants across the tree, which the fold enforces.
  • Limits. No first-come-first-served order can be imposed on folders, only conditions; and a request still carries one write.

docs.title: Formal model and audits
docs.text:
As someone who will implement or rely on this design, I want to know exactly which guarantees are proved, how the proofs were checked, and what is not covered, so that I do not mistake a modelled property for an implemented one.

The design is modelled in Lean 4 under lean/MpfsCage/RequestApprovalFold/. The proofs establish properties of the model. They do not establish that the validators implement it: no validator implements it yet, and conformance is a separate milestone ticket (#114).

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
Part What it captures Trie, writes, conditions The tree as a map from keys to entries; set and unset; absent, present and equals, read on the logical tree, the tree with every witness removed; ordered application within a fold Durable witness A witnessed entry holding the attested value or absence, the deposit and the refund address, with one witness token in its own output at the registry state's address, bound to the request that issued it Registry state Registry identity, oracle identities, protocol hash, optional rule, tree, one fee balance per key, and a value equal to the sum of the balances Request output Registry, owner, seed, a fresh output reference, one write, conditions, a fee per oracle, deadline, window, evidence, escrow, its request token and one tag per oracle Judgment Registry, request, oracle identity, verdict, the record of the members that signed and, for an approval, the oracle's own conditions, all bound in its name Claim A claim token named after the registry, the claiming key, the destination address and datum of the payout, a deadline and a tip Price notice An oracle identity's price token and its current fee, optionally per protocol Extraction A request that names a key and the value or absence it wants witnessed, with its deposit, refund address, remainder, deadline and window, and no oracle fees Transactions Creation, judgment, fold, owner withdrawal, claim creation, claim withdrawal, extraction creation, extraction withdrawal, judgment burn, and price notice minting and update, each with its guard Fold items A write request, a complete account, a claim, an extraction and the complete account of an extraction, each applied to the state the previous item left, under one validity interval that fits every item Step The authoritative transition relation over a global state, labelled by the exact transaction performed

Modelling choices the decisions left open, ruled before the model was written: a registry has at least one oracle or a rule, and no repeated oracle; the rule is an abstract predicate over one request and the creating transaction's signatures; each oracle has its own non-negative fee; creation requires escrow covering the sum of the fees plus the ledger minimum, a fixed positive parameter of the registry; time is a single observed value whose soundness against transaction validity intervals is assumed; names are collision-free structured values, standing for the hashes the implementation will use.

Readings of the money decisions, ruled before the fee balances were stated:

  • conservation counts the registry's value on both sides: its value before, plus the request escrows and claim escrows, equals its value after, plus the request remainders, claim payouts and claim tips; the registry's permanent minimum reserve is outside this account;
  • a claim output holds its tip, which goes to the folder when the claim is folded and back to the claiming key on withdrawal; a claim folds strictly before its deadline and is withdrawn from its deadline on, so there is no gap;
  • a complete account pays the same total per oracle, and the same remainder to the owner, whichever verdicts are shown; when a group judged more than once with different signers, the folder's choice of judgment decides which of its keys are credited.

Readings of the durable witness decisions, ruled before the witnesses were stated:

  • a witness carries a declared deposit of at least the ledger minimum, which funds its output and is refunded exactly;
  • an extraction is an ordinary request: it pays the folder its remainder and covers the ledger minimum at creation, declares no oracle fees, passes no rule, and keeps the three windows of every request; a request that never mints its witness returns the deposit to its owner;
  • a witness is burned only by a fold item that changes its key's value, and then its deposit goes to its refund address; a write of the value already held keeps it, and a witnessing set of the value already witnessed is not folded;
  • the issuer has no exit: no signature, deadline or withdrawal releases a live witness or its deposit;
  • items are applied in order, so a fold that changes a key and changes it back burns the witness at the first change; a witness minted and burned inside one fold nets out on the transaction, and its issuer is still refunded;
  • a witness of presence is a witness of an exact value read as presence: an extraction names the value it wants witnessed, and any value change burns it.

Decisions not yet in the registry model

Slots (#129) were drafted after this model was audited.

docs.title: How it was checked
docs.text:
Two independent audits ran on the first candidate, and fresh ones on the repair. Each auditor worked on a frozen copy with a sealed list of inputs and never contacted the author.

flowchart LR
  c1["First candidate<br/>46 theorems"] --> a1["Statement audit:<br/>two theorems weaker than the decisions"]
  c1 --> m1["Mutation audit:<br/>six guards no theorem protected"]
  a1 --> d["New rulings:<br/>one exit per window,<br/>equivocation accepted"]
  m1 --> r["Repair:<br/>60 theorems"]
  d --> r
  r --> a2["Statement audit: passed"]
  r --> m2["Mutation audit:<br/>no surviving mutant"]
  a2 --> x["Extension: tags per oracle,<br/>price notices, role-led names<br/>78 theorems"]
  m2 --> x
  x --> a3["Statement audit: passed"]
  x --> m3["Mutation audit:<br/>no surviving mutant"]
Audit First candidate Repaired candidate Statements and proofs: does each theorem say what the decisions promise, is it reachable, is it proved? Two failures: the legal-exit theorem did not bind the exit to the actual removal, and the approval-disclosure theorem relied on an assumption no decision granted Passed on every row except the independent blind reading of the statements, which was not commissioned Mutations: does breaking the model make a theorem fail? Six model changes passed every theorem: forged judgment references at the fold and at settlement, a request for a foreign registry, a diverted remainder, swapped fees, a burn that kept the token, a duplicate request in a fold 98 single-edit mutants; none passes the full build; 59 of 60 theorems are each killed by a relevant mutant

The extension for tags per oracle, price notices and role-led names was audited the same way: the statement and proof audit passed every row except the uncommissioned blind reading, and the mutation audit ran 100 single-edit mutants, none of which passes the full build; 75 of 78 theorems are each killed by a relevant mutant.

flowchart LR
  y["Extension: rules, request tokens,<br/>oracle conditions<br/>111 theorems"] --> a4["Statement audit:<br/>two theorems too weak"]
  y --> m4["Mutation audit:<br/>rule input and policy unprotected"]
  a4 --> z["Repair:<br/>113 theorems"]
  m4 --> z
  z --> a5["Statement audit: passed"]
  z --> m5["Mutation audit:<br/>no surviving mutant"]

The extension for registry rules, request tokens, registries without oracles, the present condition and oracle conditions needed one repair. The statement audit found the dead-judgment burn theorem limited to approvals without conditions, and the rule-burn theorem true by definition. The mutation audit found that a rule fed a different request or different signatures, or a request token minted by the release policy despite a rule, broke no theorem. The repair restated the first two theorems over the actual transitions and added theorems binding the rule to the created request and the creating signatures, and the request token to the rule's policy. On the repair, the statement and proof audit passed every row except the uncommissioned blind reading, and the mutation audit ran 145 single-edit mutants, none of which passes the full build; 105 of 113 theorems are each killed by a relevant mutant.

What the mutation audit could not count as killed, none of it a defect:

  • the theorem that the windows cover all time is arithmetic over time alone, so no change to the model can falsify it; the timing of each exit is protected separately;
  • a mutant that forbids an oracle from answering both ways does falsify the equivocation theorem, as a separate proof shows, but the build fails first in the examples, so the strict rule of the audit leaves it uncounted.
  • the theorems that tags are unique per request and that discovery works across registries are each guarded by an earlier theorem that the relevant mutant breaks first (registry validity, and discovery itself), so the fault is caught but not credited to them;
  • in the same way, discovery of requests across registries, the burn of the request token on every removal, the need for a rule in a registry without oracles, and the uselessness of a stale approval are each guarded by an earlier theorem (request-token discovery, the burn of tags on every exit, the impossibility of a registry with neither oracles nor rule, and the fold proving every condition) that the relevant mutant breaks first.

flowchart TB
  c1["138 statements"] --> a1["Statement audit:<br/>claim history unbound,<br/>approval lookup weakened"]
  a1 --> c2["Repair: 141 statements"]
  c2 --> a2["Statement audit:<br/>equivocation weakened"]

Wiring oracle identities, fee balances, complete accounts and claims into the registry model restated 90 of the 113 earlier theorems and added 29. Every audit read the statements blind before comparing them with the decisions, and compared each restated theorem with its earlier form, so that no guarantee was weakened under a kept name.

The first statement audit found that the theorem on claim signatures did not tie a live claim to its own history: a model that created claims unsigned, or changed a claim's payout after creation, satisfied every statement. It also found the approval lookup reduced to a list membership true by definition, and fifteen earlier theorems weaker than before. The repair bound every live claim to a signed creation on the state's own history and restored the rest. The second audit found the equivocation theorem no longer tied to a live request of the state's registry, and no statement that the exit windows do not overlap. After that repair the third audit found every statement exact, each of the 142 falsified by at least one single-edit mutant, and 155 of 157 listed guards and effects killed. The other two are equivalent mutants: an interval check that the fold already makes.

All 142 theorems were then proved without changing any statement. An independent proof audit confirmed the elaborated types identical to the audited statements, no escape hatch, only the standard axioms, and read the money proofs against reachable examples.

Adding durable witnesses kept all 142 earlier theorems, restated 21 of them over the new transitions and added 57. The first statement audit found a supporting lemma on fold payments false once an extraction met a witnessed key, and no statement that a consumed extraction leaves for good: a model that let its owner withdraw the same escrow forever satisfied every theorem. The repair stated extraction terminality as for ordinary requests. The second audit found that a model recording a fold's witness events in reverse order, so that a witness could be consumed before the item that minted it, also satisfied every theorem; the repair stated that witness events follow item order. The third audit read every statement blind, killed a single-edit mutant for each of the 199 theorems, including a burn on a same-value write, a burn on a write to another key, an issuer-signed burn, a refund to the wrong address and an extraction without its tip, and replayed all 392 mutants in clean trees. One guard, an interval check the fold already makes, is an equivalent mutant.

All 199 theorems were then proved without changing any statement. An independent proof audit confirmed the elaborated types and their dependencies identical to the audited statements, replayed every proof in a fresh kernel check, found no escape hatch and only the standard axioms, and read the witness and money proofs against reachable examples.

What this model does not cover: the hash and encoding of a description, and the cost of authorization and splitting. The registry model binds the record of signers to each judgment and credits fees by it.

docs.title: Request lifecycle
docs.text:
As a requester, I want to know at every moment which single exit can end my request, so that no race between parties decides its fate.

A request lives from its creation until exactly one of three exits consumes it: a fold applying it, a fold settling it by complete account, or the owner's withdrawal. Which exit is possible depends only on the time, measured against the request's own deadline and window, both chosen by the requester.

docs.title: States of a request
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Pending: requester creates it,<br/>spends the seed, mints the tags
  Pending --> Folded: fold, before the deadline,<br/>with an approval from every oracle
  Pending --> Settled: fold item in the window: complete account,<br/>with a verdict from every oracle
  Pending --> Withdrawn: owner, after the window
  Folded --> [*]: write applied, fees credited,<br/>remainder to the folder, tags burned
  Settled --> [*]: fees credited, remainder to the owner,<br/>tags burned
  Withdrawn --> [*]: everything to the owner,<br/>tags burned
  note left of Pending
    Oracles mint approvals and refusals
    by reference: the request does not move
  end note

Judging never moves the request: each oracle mints its verdict into its own wallet with the request output as a reference input. A request with several oracles therefore has no contention while it is being judged.

  foldw -- "deadline" --> settlew["Deadline to deadline plus window<br/><b>only a fold settling it</b><br/>by complete account"]
  settlew -- "deadline plus window" --> withdraww["After the window<br/><b>only the owner's withdrawal</b>"]
Window The only exit What it needs Who is paid Before the deadline Fold An approval from every oracle of the registry (or the oracle's signature on the fold), and every condition true against the tree at that point of the fold Every oracle's fee credited to its balance; the folder the remainder From the deadline to the deadline plus the window, both included Complete account, as an item of a fold A verdict from every oracle, approvals and refusals in any mix Every oracle's fee credited to its balance; the owner the remainder After the window Owner's withdrawal The owner's signature The owner everything

The windows are disjoint and together cover all time, so exactly one exit is possible at any moment. Several folders may still compete for the same registry state, but the outcome for the request never depends on who submits first: a complete account pays the same whichever verdicts it shows.

A refusal is therefore no early exit. It is the signed record of why the oracle declined, and the evidence a complete account needs; a refused request waits for its deadline, which its requester chose.

docs.title: Creating a request
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant R as Requester
  participant G as Registry rule (if any)
  participant P as Request script (release-wide)
  participant C as Registry state
  R->>G: mint the request token: the rule checks the write,<br/>conditions and owner of this one request
  R->>P: spend the seed output, mint one tag per oracle, each named after its oracle
  P->>C: read the registry state by reference (the registry exists)
  P-->>R: tags minted only if escrow covers the oracles' fees<br/>plus the minimum for a refund output
  R->>P: request output: registry, owner, seed, one write,<br/>conditions, fee per oracle, deadline, window, evidence

The seed is an output reference spent by the creating transaction. No two requests in history can carry the same seed, so no judgment can ever be replayed onto a copied request.

docs.title: Judging
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant O as Oracle
  participant P as Request script (minting policy)
  participant Q as Request output
  O->>O: judge the request off chain under the registry's protocol
  O->>P: mint approval or refusal, signed by the oracle
  P->>Q: read the request by reference (it is live, before its deadline)
  P-->>O: token named after registry, request with seed, oracle and verdict

An oracle may also skip the separate judgment and sign the fold itself; its signature counts as its approval of every request in that fold. A registry with one oracle that folds its own requests therefore needs one transaction per batch, as the shipped cage does.

docs.title: Folding
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant F as Folder
  participant C as Registry state
  participant Q as Request outputs
  participant J as Judgment tokens
  F->>Q: spend the chosen requests, in the chosen order
  F->>J: read one approval per oracle per request (by reference),<br/>with each oracle's conditions
  F->>C: for each request: prove the requester's and the oracles' conditions<br/>against the current tree, apply its write
  C-->>F: new root, with oracles and protocol unchanged
  C-->>F: every oracle's fee credited to its keys' balances in the registry state
  F->>F: keep the remainders, burn the tags

The folder chooses which approved requests to fold and in what order. It cannot apply an unapproved request, change a write, skip a request it consumed, or fold the same request twice.

docs.title: Settling and withdrawing
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant F as Any folder
  participant W as Owner
  participant C as Registry state
  participant Q as Request output
  participant J as Judgment tokens
  Note over F,J: from the deadline to the deadline plus the window
  F->>Q: spend the request as an item of a fold
  F->>J: read one verdict per oracle (approval or refusal)
  F->>C: credit every oracle's fee to its keys' balances
  F-->>W: the remainder, in one refund output
  Note over W,Q: after the window
  W->>Q: spend the request with the owner's signature
  W-->>W: take everything, burn the tags

The complete account is an item of a fold because it credits fees, and only a fold changes the registry state. It earns the folder nothing, so the parties that want it folded are the owner, waiting for its refund, and the oracles, waiting for their fees; folding is permissionless, so either can fold it. A fold may mix complete accounts with writes and claims as long as its validity interval fits every item's window.

After the window the chain cannot tell a silent oracle from an approval the owner chooses not to show, so the owner takes everything and decides whether to pay the oracles that answered. A silent oracle loses its fee; that is the price of not answering. The withdrawal does not touch the registry state.

docs.title: Claiming fees
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant K as Key oracle
  participant P as Request script (release-wide)
  participant F as Any folder
  participant C as Registry state
  K->>P: create a claim: mint the claim token with the key's signature,<br/>name the payout address and datum, add a tip
  F->>C: fold the claim at its turn
  C-->>K: the key's whole balance, to exactly that address and datum
  F-->>F: keep the tip, burn the claim token

A claim is a request without a write. The oracle chooses when to claim, so it pays the ledger's minimum for an output once per claim, out of fees that have grown large enough, instead of once per oracle per request. A folder may leave a claim out; the oracle can then fold it itself. A claim not folded by its deadline goes back to the oracle.

docs.title: Dead judgments
docs.text: Once a request has been consumed its seed can never occur again, so any judgment still naming it is worthless. Its holder may burn it at any time, without the request or the registry state taking part.

docs.title: Open MPFS: design document
docs.text:
As anyone who wants a shared, verifiable key-value registry on Cardano, I want to create one by naming the oracles that judge it and the checks they perform, so that the registry needs no owner, no script of its own and no folding infrastructure, its rules can never be changed under its users, and anyone can fold what its oracles have approved.

This document gathers the decisions taken from 24 to 27 October 2026 on open MPFS: Merkle Patricia Forestry registries without an owner, judged by independent oracles and folded by anyone. Each section says what is decided, what is a draft whose direction is agreed but whose details are still moving, and what is open.

Status Meaning Decided Recorded in the decision records; the earlier part is modelled in Lean and audited Draft Direction agreed in discussion; details may still change Open Not decided

The decision records are the authority; this document explains them:

  • specs/request-approval-fold/decisions.md: requests, judgments, folds and money;
  • specs/oracle-identity/decisions.md: oracle identities and how fees reach keys;
  • specs/oracle-slots/decisions.md: slots and check protocols, the draft.
  • specs/durable-witnesses/decisions.md: durable witnesses of registry facts.

docs.title: Shared state needs folding
docs.text:
The hard problem here is not the Merkle Patricia Forestry. It is shared state on Cardano.

A registry is one piece of state that many people want to change. On Cardano that state lives in a single output, and changing it means spending that output and creating its successor. Only one transaction can spend an output. If two people each build a transaction that updates the registry, the first one in a block wins and the other is rejected, because the output it spent no longer exists. With many writers, almost every direct update would fail.

With a Merkle Patricia Forestry it is worse. A write carries a proof built against the root the writer last saw. When another update lands first, the root changes and the proof is stale: the loser must fetch the new tree, rebuild its proof and race again, against everyone else doing the same.

So writers do not touch the state, and do not build proofs. Each writer creates a request in an output of its own, where it contends with nobody. Then one transaction spends the state together with a batch of requests and applies them all, in order, producing the next state. That transaction is a fold.

flowchart LR
  a([Writer A]) -- "own output" --> ra[(Request A)]
  b([Writer B]) -- "own output" --> rb[(Request B)]
  c([Writer C]) -- "own output" --> rc[(Request C)]
  ra & rb & rc --> fold["Fold: one transaction<br/>applies the batch in order"]
  s0[(State n)] -- "spent once" --> fold
  fold --> s1[(State n + 1)]

The folder builds every proof at fold time, one after another, each against the root left by the previous write, so the proofs are right by construction. A writer only states its write and the conditions it expects of the tree; the folder proves them. The Merkle Patricia Forestry makes the state small enough to live in one output, a root hash, and makes each write checkable with a short proof; any shared state on Cardano, with or without a tree, needs the same folding pattern.

Folding answers contention and raises two questions in its place: who folds, and who decides which requests may be folded. MPFS today answers both with one key. Open MPFS answers them with services anyone can run.

docs.title: Why open MPFS
docs.text: MPFS today is a registry with a keeper. One key owns the cage, judges every request, and is the only party allowed to fold. The design makes the keeper unable to cheat the tree, but not unnecessary: every write waits for it, every rule lives in its private code, and running it is a cost its operator carries for the sake of its own application. Open MPFS turns that keeper into a set of services anyone can offer and be paid for. Two experiences led here.

docs.title: What moog taught
docs.text:
Moog runs its registry on the shipped cage. Reading what its oracle actually checks shows five things.

flowchart LR
  req([Requesters]) -- "requests with a tip" --> op["One operator key:<br/>owner, oracle and folder"]
  op -- "runs off chain" --> checks["Moog's checks:<br/>signatures, tree facts, GitHub"]
  op -- "the only one who can fold,<br/>end or sweep the cage" --> cage[(Cage)]
  agent([Moog agent]) -- "results, trusted by the operator" --> op
  • One key does three jobs. The owner is the oracle and the only folder; it can also end the cage. If its operator stops, nothing moves, and nobody else may step in.
  • Every check is off chain, in one program, even those the chain could make. The oracle checks the requester's signature, that a role or a white-listing exists, that test runs are numbered in order, that results come from the agent. The chain could check all of these with signatures and tree conditions; instead readers trust that one program ran them. Only the GitHub lookups truly need an oracle.
  • Generic checks are locked inside one application. "This GitHub user publishes this key" and "this repository's code owners name this user" are useful to many registries, but they exist only as moog's oracle code, run by moog's operator, for moog.
  • Running the oracle is a cost, not a business. The requester's tip pays for the folding transaction. The operator runs the oracle because it needs the registry, so nobody outside the application has a reason to run one, and nobody can compete to run it better or cheaper.
  • Unaccepted requests are never refused. Moog's oracle has no refusal: a request it will not accept stays in the cage, checked again at every poll, until its owner retracts it, and the requester learns nothing about why.

docs.title: What permissionless Singular taught
docs.text:
Singular, a permissionless mint of unique names over a Merkle Patricia Forestry registry, went through the same move first.

  • Anyone can fold, from public data alone. Singular's folds need no signer and no privileged folder; the request's remainder is the folder's bid, so folding is a market instead of a duty.
  • No one keeps power over a registry after creating it. Singular has no authority to update parameters or migrate a registry; whoever could would hold power over every name in it.
  • What a creator declares unchecked becomes an attack. Singular's creators wrote policy references into the registry that creation did not check, and a forged one let someone mint a live name outside any fold. Everything a creator declares must either be checked or be the registry's identity, named by hash.
  • Admission belongs to the application, not to the protocol. Singular's investigation (lambdasistemi/singular#731, #741) moved the request lifecycle out of the protocol and into the application, which keeps the protocol small and provable. In open MPFS the application is the registry's rule and its oracles; the protocol only folds what they admitted. Open MPFS keeps one generic request lifecycle for every registry, because oracles must be paid for judging even when nothing is written.
  • No state outside the tree. Per-key tokens held outside Singular's registry were where its forgeries lived; open MPFS keeps everything in the tree.

docs.title: From a keeper to services
docs.text:
MPFS today Open MPFS Who may fold The owner Anyone, paid by the request's remainder Who judges The owner's oracle Independent oracles, named per slot, each paid per judgment Where the rules are One private program Signatures in the rule, tree facts in conditions, only outside-world facts in oracles Who can change or end the registry The owner No one A request that is not accepted Waits until its owner retracts it Refused and paid for, with the refusal on chain Why someone runs an oracle To have their own registry To earn fees from every registry that names it Reusing a check Copy the code Name the same check protocol and provider

The parties who care about a registry each run the piece they are good at, in the service of requesters. A team that needs a registry declares its rule and picks its providers, once. Whoever can verify something about the world, such as a GitHub identity, publishes a check and serves it to every registry that wants it, for a fee. Whoever runs an indexer and a node folds, for the remainder. Requesters pay each of them for exactly the work done, and no one of them can stop, redirect or rewrite the others.

docs.title: The system at a glance
docs.text:
Two words carry the whole design. A registry is a key-value database together with its rules: what users create, write to and read. Its registry state is the one output on chain, marked by a unique token, that holds the database's root hash, its slots, protocol and rule, and the oracles' fee balances. The database itself lives off chain, rebuilt by anyone from the writes recorded on chain. The shipped design calls the registry state the cage.

flowchart LR
  creator([Registry creator]) -- "mints, naming slots,<br/>protocol and rule" --> state[(Registry state:<br/>root, slots, balances)]
  requester([Requester]) -- "creates request: write,<br/>conditions, evidence, fees" --> request[(Request output)]
  oracle([Oracle]) -- "judges off chain,<br/>mints approval or refusal" --> judgment[(Judgment token)]
  folder([Folder]) -- "spends requests, reads judgments,<br/>proves conditions" --> state
  request -- "spent by exactly one exit" --> folder
  judgment -. "read by reference" .-> folder
  reader([Reader]) -- "replays folds" --> state

The shipped cage has one owner that alone folds requests, and one request script per cage. Open MPFS removes both. A registry is data naming its judges; one request script per release serves every registry; folding is a service anyone can offer and be paid for.

Who Wants Does Registry creator A registry whose rules are fixed forever Names the slots, the protocol and the rule, once Requester One write applied under conditions they choose Creates a request carrying the write, the conditions, the evidence and the fees Oracle To be paid for judging Judges off chain, mints an approval or a refusal, collects its fees by claim Folder The remainder of the requests it folds Applies approved requests to the tree, proving their conditions Reader The registry's contents Rebuilds the tree by replaying folds; every write is on chain

docs.title: Registries
docs.text:
Decided.

  • Anyone can create a registry. Creation mints the registry state with an empty root, the oracles, the protocol and optionally a rule. No script is applied to a registry.
  • A registry needs at least one oracle or a rule. A registry with neither would accept any write.
  • Everything is declared at creation and never changes. Whoever could change a part would hold power over everyone who trusted the registry. The oracles and the protocol are the registry's identity: new judges mean a new, empty registry.
  • A registry has no owner and no end. Its oracles are its only judges. A registry whose oracles stop answering stops moving.
  • Oracles need not consent to being named. Naming is an offer of business; an oracle that does not want it never answers.

docs.title: Who checks what
docs.text:
Decided, with the slot row a draft. A registry defends itself in four layers, each blind to what another sees:

Layer Runs Defends against Blind to Rule Once, when the request is created The wrong writer (signatures), malformed writes, writes without the conditions they need (it demands them) The tree and the outside world Conditions At the fold, at the request's turn Stale, out-of-order or duplicated writes Anything not in the tree Oracles in slots Off chain, attested by a judgment False claims about the outside world Keys outside their slots The fold Every fold Forged requests, late folds, altered bytes, missing approvals, false conditions Meaning: it checks bytes, hashes and proofs

Under all four lies immutability: no one can switch them off later.

  • An oracle is needed only where the chain cannot see the data. Signatures belong to the rule; facts about earlier writes are conditions; only the outside world needs an oracle.
  • A service that only reports its own work is a key in the rule, not an oracle. Its writes are trusted because it signed them; the registry limits where it may write and that it cannot overwrite.
  • The equals condition ties a signer to the tree. A rule can demand "the user's registered key equals the key that signed", so an earlier registration authorizes a later request with no oracle.
  • Rules are compiled minting policies, named by hash in the registry state, minting the request token, so they run exactly once, at creation, on one request. They reach the tree only by demanding conditions.
  • The condition language is absent, present and equals, each costing one Merkle Patricia Forestry proof in the fold.

docs.title: Requests
docs.text:
Decided.

  • A request carries one write, set key value or unset key, on chain in its datum, so readers rebuild the tree for free.
  • A request carries conditions, checked at the fold against the tree at its turn. Compare-and-swap is a write with a condition on its own key.
  • A request carries evidence, opaque to the chain; the protocol decides whether it holds the evidence or its hash.
  • A request carries a seed, an output spent by its creation, so no two requests in history are equal and no judgment can be replayed.
  • A request carries a deadline and a window, which divide its life into three periods, each with exactly one exit.
  • A request carries one request token, minted by the rule or the release policy at creation. It is what makes a request genuine; folders find a registry's live requests with one query by it.
  • A request carries one tag per oracle, named after the oracle, so an oracle finds all its work across every registry with one query.
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Pending: created, seed spent,<br/>request token and tags minted
  Pending --> Folded: fold before the deadline,<br/>with every approval it needs
  Pending --> Settled: complete account in the window,<br/>a verdict from every oracle
  Pending --> Withdrawn: owner, after the window
  Folded --> [*]: write applied, fees credited,<br/>remainder to the folder
  Settled --> [*]: fees credited,<br/>remainder to the owner
  Withdrawn --> [*]: everything to the owner
Period The only exit Who is paid Before the deadline A fold applying the write Oracles their fees; the folder the remainder From the deadline to the deadline plus the window A fold settling it by complete account Oracles their fees; the owner the remainder After the window The owner's withdrawal The owner everything

docs.title: Judgments
docs.text:
Decided, with the trimmed minting checks a draft.

  • An oracle approves or refuses by minting a token under the release policy, by reference to the request. Nothing is spent, so oracles never contend for an output.
  • The policy computes the token's name from the registry, the complete request datum, the oracle, the verdict, the members of a group oracle that signed and, for an approval, the oracle's conditions. The oracle chooses its verdict, its conditions and who signs; it cannot produce a name for content it did not see.
  • An approval may carry the oracle's conditions, the assumptions it judged under; the fold proves them at the request's turn.
  • A fold signed by an oracle counts as its approval, so an oracle that folds itself needs no separate judgment.
  • Approving and refusing pay the same, so an oracle gains nothing by its verdict.
  • Equivocation is accepted. An oracle can mint both verdicts; under the periods above it changes nothing, and both stay on chain under its signature.
  • Draft: minting checks only what the fold cannot. The policy needs the preimage of the name, to see which oracle it claims; the oracle's authorization; and a time before the request's deadline, so that no oracle is paid by a complete account for a judgment made too late. Whether the oracle belongs to the registry is left to the fold, which matches names against its own slots. A judgment then needs no reference to the registry state, which every fold spends, so judging never races folding.
sequenceDiagram
  participant R as Requester
  participant O as Oracle
  participant F as Folder
  participant C as Registry state
  R->>R: create request: write, conditions, evidence, fees, seed
  O->>O: parse under its check, look at the world
  O->>O: mint approval named after the exact request datum
  F->>C: fold: genuine request, on time, approvals of every matching slot,<br/>conditions proved, write applied, fees credited

What the fold checks for each request, in order:

  1. The request carries the registry's request token, and the fold's validity interval falls before its deadline.
  2. Which slots match: each slot whose prefix starts the written key, by byte comparison. No CDDL is read on chain.
  3. For each matching slot, a judgment token whose name the fold recomputes from the request it spends, the slot's oracle and the conditions and signers given in the redeemer; or that oracle's authorization of the fold.
  4. Every condition, the requester's and each approval's, against the tree at this turn, by proof.
  5. The new root after the write.
  6. Each matching slot's fee, credited to the signers of its judgment.

docs.title: Money
docs.text:
Decided.

  • The request pays for judgment, not for outcome, declaring a fee per oracle.
  • Fees accumulate in the registry state. Paying each oracle in its own output would cost the ledger's minimum per oracle per request. The registry state keeps a balance per key and holds their sum.
  • Only a fold spends the registry state. Everything that changes it is an item of a fold, so nothing races the fold:
Fold item When Effect Write request Before its deadline Applies the write, credits the fees, remainder to the folder Complete account In its window Writes nothing, credits the fees, remainder to the owner Claim Before its deadline Pays one key's whole balance to the destination the claim names
  • An oracle collects its fees by claim, a request created with its key's signature that names the payout address and datum. The folder cannot choose the payout; the fold checks it exactly.
  • The escrow exceeds the fees by the ledger's minimum, so a complete account can always refund the owner.
flowchart LR
  req([Request escrow]) -- "fee per oracle" --> cage[(Registry state: one balance per key)]
  req -- "remainder" --> folder([Folder, or the owner<br/>on a complete account])
  cage -- "claim: whole balance" --> payout([Payout chosen by the key])

docs.title: Oracle identities
docs.text:
Decided. The oracle identity is a standard of its own, which open MPFS consumes and which may move to its own repository.

  • An oracle is a key or a group: a threshold and members, each a key or a group, each with a share. Groups nest.
  • Its identity is the hash of its description and never changes. Keys are not rotated: a group that loses members beyond its threshold is dead, and its users name a new identity in a new registry.
  • A key authorizes by signing; a group when its threshold of members authorize, recursively. The description travels in the redeemer; one library function checks it for every contract, rules included.
  • Only the members that signed are paid, by their shares, down to keys. The signers are bound in the judgment's name. The integer remainder goes to the first signer.
  • A key stolen compromises only its oracles, up to their thresholds. A registry naming several oracles already needs all of them; a single oracle protects itself with a group.
flowchart TD
  group["Group oracle, threshold 2"] -- "share 2" --> alice["Key: Alice"]
  group -- "share 1" --> bob["Key: Bob"]
  group -- "share 1" --> inner["Group oracle, threshold 1"]
  inner -- "share 1" --> carol["Key: Carol"]
  inner -- "share 1" --> dave["Key: Dave"]

If Alice and Carol sign a judgment whose fee is 9, Alice is paid 6 and Carol 3; Bob and Dave, who did not sign, are paid nothing.

docs.title: Slots and check protocols
docs.text:
Draft, except where marked decided.

  • A registry names its oracles in slots: an oracle identity, the hash of a check protocol, a key prefix and parameters.
  • A write needs approval only from the slots whose prefix matches its key. Keys under no slot are gated by the rule alone; a registry without a rule refuses them. When several slots match, all must approve.
  • A check protocol is a document named by hash, published by whoever writes the checking software: what is checked, the parameters, the shape of the key after the prefix and of the value, in CDDL. A new version is a new hash.
  • Under a slot's prefix the registry imports the check's shapes; the rule may only narrow them.
  • A registry protocol ships a request zoo, one sample per kind of request, validated before creation against each slot's check, its parameters and the rule. A passing zoo means the registry engages its checks correctly.
  • An oracle reads slots, not registry documents. It engages a slot when it implements its check, accepts its parameters and the fee meets its price.
  • Decided: liveness is incentivized, not enforced. A silent oracle stalls its slots and nothing replaces it, since a fallback judge would reintroduce an owner. Answering is what earns. A creator protects a registry by choosing providers, or by naming a group of competing providers whose threshold trades liveness against agreement.
  • Decided: creating a registry is a challenge to its oracles. Nothing is negotiated beforehand; a slot proves to be served when its kinds of request are judged. A creator probes each slot and abandons a silent registry at the cost of its creation.

With slots, "every oracle" in the sections above reads "every oracle whose slot matches the key": tags, approvals, complete accounts and fees follow the matching slots.

docs.title: Worked example: moog
docs.text:
Moog lets GitHub users request test runs on Antithesis. Its registry splits into three GitHub slots and two prefixes gated by its rule alone:

flowchart LR
  write([A write]) --> match{"Key prefix"}
  match -- "user/github/" --> s1["GitHub oracle:<br/>key file check"]
  match -- "role/github/" --> s2["GitHub oracle:<br/>code owners role check"]
  match -- "run/github/" --> s3["GitHub oracle:<br/>compose assets check"]
  match -- "white/github/, state/github/" --> rule["Rule alone:<br/>the agent signs"]

A test run needs the GitHub oracle only to confirm that the commit and its compose file exist. That the requester holds the role, that the repository is white-listed, that the requester's registered key signed and that runs are numbered in order are conditions and rule checks. The agent's acceptances and results need no oracle: the rule checks the agent's signature and a condition checks the previous state. The CDDL for the slots, the checks and the moog protocol is on Oracle slots and check protocols.

docs.title: Durable witnesses
docs.text:
Decided.

A consumer proving a fact about one key references the registry state and its root. A fold writing any other key spends that output and changes the root, so the consumer must rebuild its proof although its fact still holds. Durable witnesses remove that dependence on unrelated writes.

  • A witness attests one fact about one key: absent, present, or holding an exact value.
  • Anyone extracts one by funding its deposit, and is its issuer.
  • It stays usable until the next change to its key. Writes to other keys leave it usable and its deposit in place.
  • The registry tracks the obligation per key, and every fold complies. The next change to a tracked key consumes its witness and refunds the deposit to the issuer in the same fold; otherwise the fold is invalid. A value change consumes a presence witness even when the key stays present.
  • A key has at most one witness, kept in the trie. A key is unwitnessed, holding its value or with no entry when absent, or witnessed, when its entry is the witness: the attested value or absence and the refund address. A witnessed absence reads as absent to conditions and readers.
  • Extraction is a request that needs only its deposit, with no rule and no oracle, folded like a write, that turns the key's entry into a witness. The next set or unset on the key proves that entry, burns the witness and pays the deposit to the refund address.
  • Extraction commits to the value it wants, or to absence, and is folded only when the key is unwitnessed and holds exactly that at its turn.
  • The folder burns, writes and mints in one transaction. It burns the old witness token, changes the tree and, when the request asks, mints the new witness token, so a witnessed entry always has exactly one live token.
  • Witness tokens sit at the registry state's address, each in its own output funded by its deposit. A consumer references it; only a fold spends it.
  • A set request can include the witnessing: it writes the value and leaves the key witnessed with it, refunding any earlier witness in the same fold.
  • The deposit is separate from oracle fees, the folder's remainder and the request owner's refund.
  • A witness attests what the registry records; its outside-world meaning still rests on the rule and the oracles.
flowchart TB
  issuer([Anyone]) -- "extracts, funds deposit" --> live[Witness outstanding:<br/>key tracks the obligation]
  live -- "used as evidence" --> consumer([Consumer contract])
  live -- "next change<br/>to this key" --> fold[One fold: changes the key,<br/>consumes the witness,<br/>refunds the issuer]
  fold -- "result" --> done[Old witness unusable,<br/>deposit returned]

This follows Singular's second product milestone, whose presence, absent and terminal witnesses introduced proof durability.

docs.title: Status and open questions
docs.text:
The decisions up to 26 October, the request, judgment and fold design with rules and request tokens, are modelled in Lean and audited; see Formal model and audits. The decisions of 27 October are not modelled yet: oracle identities, fees in the registry state, complete accounts and claims as fold items, durable witnesses, slots and the trimmed minting checks. Nothing is implemented in the validators yet.

Open:

  • Whether prices are announced per check protocol, listing every provider of a check in one query, instead of per oracle.
  • Whether the fee is declared per matching slot, and whether a judgment's name binds the slot, for an oracle in two slots matching one key.
  • Whether oracles attest facts independently of any registry, valid until an expiry, so that one judgment of a world fact serves every registry that uses the same check; this would need its own payment path.
  • The cost of prefix matching, condition proofs and fee splits in the fold, to be measured on a devnet.
  • The migration or coexistence of existing cages.

docs.title: Oracle identities
docs.text:
As someone running an oracle, alone or with others, I want one on-chain identity that any contract can name and check, so that a contract naming me acts only on my authorization, and so that when I share the work with other oracles each of us knows its share of the fees before serving.

An oracle's key can be stolen. With one key per oracle, a stolen key is a stolen oracle: the thief can approve whatever the oracle could. A registry that names several oracles already needs every one of them to approve a write, so one stolen oracle there can only block requests, never write. A registry with one oracle, which is how the shipped cage works, has no such protection.

The oracle identity is a standard of its own, recorded in specs/oracle-identity/decisions.md. Registries consume it; it does not depend on them.

docs.title: Keys and groups
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  group["Group oracle<br/>threshold 2<br/>identity = hash of this description"] -- "share 2" --> alice["Key oracle: Alice"]
  group -- "share 1" --> bob["Key oracle: Bob"]
  group -- "share 1" --> inner["Group oracle<br/>threshold 1"]
  inner -- "share 1" --> carol["Key oracle: Carol"]
  inner -- "share 1" --> dave["Key oracle: Dave"]

An oracle is a key, or a group: a threshold and a list of member oracles, each with a share. In the group above, any two of Alice, Bob and the inner group authorize, and the inner group authorizes when Carol or Dave signs. The group survives one stolen key, and keeps working with one member silent.

The identity is the hash of the description, so it never changes. A contract that names it trusts exactly those keys, thresholds and shares. Keys are never rotated: a group that loses members beyond its threshold is dead, and its users name a new identity in a new contract.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: A key oracle authorizes a transaction by signing it. A group authorizes it when at least its threshold of members authorize it, down to the keys. The description travels in the redeemer; the checking script hashes it, compares the hash with the identity it was given, and counts the signatures. One library function does this for every contract that consumes the standard.

docs.title: Fees
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Q as Request
  participant C as Registry balances
  participant A as Alice
  participant K as Carol
  Q->>C: fold credits a fee of 9 for a judgment signed by Alice and Carol
  Note over C: split among the signers by shares: Alice 6, inner group 3
  Note over C: inner group: 3 to Carol, its only signer. Bob and Dave get nothing
  A->>C: Alice's claim, folded when she chooses
  C-->>A: Alice's whole balance, to her payout
  K->>C: Carol's claim, later
  C-->>K: Carol's whole balance

A judgment records which members signed it, and only they are paid: the fee is split among the signers by their shares at the moment it is credited, down to keys, and each key collects its own balance by claim. No member can be cut out by the others, because the shares are part of the identity, and no member is paid for work it did not do, which matters when a group of independent providers needs only one of them. The remainder of integer division goes to the first member that signed.

No consent is needed on chain to describe a group: a member's key cannot authorize anything without its own signature, so a group naming a member that never agreed has one silent member. Serving is consent.

docs.text:
